learn.hook: Imagine a road trip where the 'highway' is a dirt track at over 5,000 metres, your car shares the plains with wild asses, and your goal is to walk around a sacred mountain.
points: Nick Middleton is a British geographer and travel writer; 'Silk Road' is an extract from his travelogue.
It records his journey across Tibet to perform the kora, the circuit around Mount Kailash; the title recalls the ancient Silk Road trade route.
He leaves Ravu with Tsetan, a skilful driver, and Daniel, who helps and translates and later heads back to Lhasa.
Landscape: open plains, the dark tents of nomads, flocks tended by solitary drokbas, a few gazelles and herds of wild asses.
Tibetan words: kora (pilgrimage circuit), drokba (nomad herder), kyang (Tibetan wild ass).

example.q: Who are Tsetan and Daniel, and what do they do?
steps: Tsetan: the hired driver who handles the tough roads.
Daniel: a travel companion who helps and translates.
Daniel later leaves to go back to Lhasa.
example.answer: Tsetan is the expert driver; Daniel is the helpful companion who leaves at Hor for Lhasa.

learn.reallife: Indian pilgrims on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, organised by the Ministry of External Affairs via Lipulekh or Nathu La, cross the same high Tibetan plateau.

topics.title: Mastiffs, a short cut and the thin air

learn.hook: At 5,515 metres, there's about half the oxygen of sea level. Your head throbs, your car slides on snow, and huge black dogs chase your wheels.
points: Tibetan mastiffs, big fearless dogs, guard nomad tents; they were prized at China's imperial courts as hunting dogs and sent as tribute along the Silk Road.
Tsetan takes a short cut heading south-west, almost directly towards Kailash, across high passes.
Snow blocks the track: Tsetan crosses one patch and drives around another, cutting off a hairpin bend; the top of the pass, at 5,515 m, is marked by a cairn of rocks.
The author suffers a throbbing headache from altitude sickness; he gulps water from his bottle on the climb, and the headache clears as they descend.

Phrases: ducking back (pulling back quickly), swathe (broad strip), careered down (moved fast, out of control), manoeuvres (skilful movements), cairn (pile of stones as a marker), salt flats (flat salty land), billowed (swelled out).

example.q: Why were Tibetan mastiffs popular in China's imperial courts?
steps: They were big, strong and fearless.
They made excellent hunting dogs.
So they were sent as tribute along the Silk Road.
example.answer: Because they were valued as powerful hunting dogs and were sent to the courts as tribute.

learn.reallife: Indian Army soldiers at Siachen and Ladakh are acclimatised for days because of altitude sickness. Drinking water and climbing slowly help, just as the author found.

learn.hook: Some places look magical in old books and disappointing in real life. Hor, on the shore of a holy lake, was one of those for the author.
points: At Hor, Daniel leaves them to hitch a ride back to Lhasa.
Hor is a grim, miserable place: no vegetation, just dust, rocks and rubbish.
The Japanese monk Ekai Kawaguchi, who reached Lake Mansarovar in 1900, was so moved by its sanctity that he burst into tears.
Contrast: the legendary, sacred beauty of Mansarovar versus the dismal reality of Hor on its shore.
Mansarovar is Tibet's most venerated lake; in Hindu and Buddhist belief it is linked with the sources of great rivers (the Sutlej actually flows from it).

example.q: Why does the author find Hor such a contrast to what Kawaguchi described?
steps: Kawaguchi found the lake spiritually overwhelming and wept.
The author finds Hor grim, dusty and littered.
The spiritual image clashes with the dirty modern town.
example.answer: Kawaguchi saw holy beauty, but the author sees a dirty, dismal town; legend and reality clash.

learn.reallife: Indian pilgrims still take a holy dip in Mansarovar on the Kailash Yatra. Like the author, many are struck by the gap between the sacred lake and the rough towns around it.

topics.title: Darchen: a cold, a doctor and Norbu

learn.hook: Stuck in a cold, dirty town with a blocked nose, unable to sleep, and no pilgrims in sight: then a stranger walks in who wants to do the same trek.
points: Darchen, at the foot of Kailash, is dirty and cold; the author has a heavy cold, a blocked nose and trouble breathing, and stays awake all night.
At Darchen's medical college a Tibetan doctor diagnoses a cold and altitude effects; Tsetan translates, and the doctor gives him a course of Tibetan medicine.
Speaking 'through' someone means communicating via an interpreter, as the author speaks to the doctor through Tsetan.
There are no pilgrims yet because the season has not begun; the author is disappointed.
He meets Norbu, a Tibetan scholar working in Beijing, who also plans the kora; when Norbu suggests going together, the author feels his 'positive thinking' has worked.

example.q: What does 'I spoke to the doctor through Tsetan' mean?
steps: The author does not speak Tibetan.

example.answer: The author communicated with the doctor with Tsetan acting as interpreter.

learn.reallife: Foreign tourists in rural India often speak 'through' a local guide who translates. The idea is the same as at Darchen.

topics.title: The kora and the meaning of the journey

learn.hook: Why would anyone walk around a mountain at over 5,000 metres? For millions of believers across four faiths, the answer is simple: Kailash is sacred.
points: Kora: the circumambulation of Mount Kailash, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of Bon.
Travel is both a physical challenge (altitude, cold, rough roads) and a spiritual quest.
Myth versus reality: legends of sacred, exotic places meet dusty towns and discomfort.
Hill people's kindness: Lhamo's farewell gift, Tsetan's care and skill, the doctor's help; and human endurance in harsh land.
Adjective-noun pairs: shaggy monsters, brackish (slightly salty) lakes, rickety (shaky) table, hairpin (very sharp) bend, rudimentary (basic) general stores.

example.q: Why is the journey both physical and spiritual?
steps: Physical: altitude sickness, snow, cold, rough tracks.
Spiritual: the goal is the kora of a sacred mountain.
The hardship itself becomes part of the pilgrimage.
example.answer: The author endures physical hardship to reach a sacred goal, so the trip tests body and spirit.

learn.reallife: The Kedarnath and Amarnath yatras show the same mix: hard climbs, cold and thin air, done out of deep faith.

learn.hook: 'Give reasons' and 'comment on' questions are where students lose marks by being vague. This lesson shows the exact points examiners want.
points: Title: refers to the old Silk Road trade routes across the region, along which goods and even Tibetan mastiffs (as tribute) travelled.

Reasons: mastiffs prized as hunting dogs; Hor disappointing against its sacred image; Darchen disappointing because of illness and no pilgrims; positive thinking 'working' when Norbu proposed teaming up.

Comments: purpose of the journey (the kora); his health at Darchen; meeting Norbu; Tsetan's steady support; Tsetan's joke that, as a Buddhist, the author's death would not matter much, but would be bad for business.
Discussion: hill folk are often kind and sensitive; people take hard journeys for faith, adventure or self-discovery; legends often differ from reality.
Long answer: travel as a test of endurance, using altitude, snow, illness and determination.

steps: Skilful driver on snowy, risky tracks.

Brings humour and calm; his Buddhist joke lightens the mood.

learn.reallife: Sherpa guides on Everest expeditions play Tsetan's role: driver, guide, translator and morale-booster rolled into one.
